stem.text: Huntington’s disease is caused by a mutation in a gene coding for a protein that has a number of cellular functions.
Identify the gene and state the name of the protein that are affected by the mutation that causes Huntington’s disease.

markScheme.note: The MS does not number these two points; n = 1, 2 is my line order (line 1 = gene answer line, line 2 = protein answer line).

explanation.text: Three different names are involved and the question only asks for two of them: the gene is HTT (gene symbols are written in italics), the protein it codes for is huntingtin, and the disease is Huntington’s disease. The answer line for the gene takes the gene, the answer line for the protein takes the protein.
On the gene line the MS accepts HTT, “huntingtin” or IT15 (IT15 is an older name for the gene). On the protein line only huntingtin is listed. The disease name is not in the MS for either line.

reasoningChain: Recall the syllabus link for this disease: HTT gene → huntingtin protein → Huntington’s disease.
Put the gene name on the “gene” line and the protein name on the “protein” line.
Do not write the disease name on either line.

stem.text: In many countries, a genetic screening test for Huntington’s disease is available.
Adults over the age of 18 years who are considered to be at risk of developing the disease are offered the genetic screening test.
Suggest which adults are considered to be at risk of developing Huntington’s disease.

topics.note: Link via the idea of a dominant allele being inherited from a parent; please confirm whether to keep.

points.text: adults that have (early) symptoms of Huntington’s ;

explanation.text: Why a family history means “at risk”: Huntington’s disease is caused by a dominant allele (MS 3(d) point 1), so a person with the disease usually has one mutant allele and one normal allele. Each of their children therefore has a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting the mutant allele. Close relatives are at risk before anyone knows their CAG repeat number.
The MS also gives the mark for adults who already show (early) symptoms of the disease.

reasoningChain: The test is offered to people who might have inherited the mutant allele.
The allele is dominant, so a child of an affected parent can inherit it from that one parent.
So adults with a (close) family history, or adults who already have early symptoms, are “at risk”.

inferredMistakes.text: Giving a general group such as “older people” or “people with a poor lifestyle”. The MS points are about inheritance (family history) or symptoms, not age or lifestyle.

stem.text: Suggest and explain why the genetic screening test for Huntington’s disease is only offered to adults who are at least 18 years old.

points.text: adult-onset disease / symptoms generally occur later in life ;

examples: e.g. whether or not to have children
e.g. at-risk parent may not have taken test
e.g. wait to see if parent has Huntington’s

points.text: psychological impact / children not able to give (informed) consent / AW ; ora

explanation.text: The question says “suggest and explain”, so each reason needs a short “because”. Possible reasons, each linked to an MS point:
• Symptoms usually appear later in life, so a test result in childhood would not change anything for the child at that age.
• An adult can decide for themselves whether they want to know, and can use the result in their own decisions, for example whether or not to have children.
• A positive result also gives information about relatives: it shows that one parent carries the allele, even if that parent chose not to be tested.
• A positive result can have a large psychological impact, and a child cannot give informed consent.
On the error the examiners name (“the genes would not have developed until later in life”): the allele is present from conception in every cell. What comes later is the symptoms, not the gene.

reasoningChain: Pick a reason from the MS ideas: later onset, the adult’s own choices, implications of a positive result, psychological impact or consent.
Add why it matters for someone under 18.
Give two different reasons for the two marks.

inferredMistakes.text: Saying only “they are adults” or “it is the law” without linking the age to consent, the person’s own life choices or the late onset of symptoms.

stem.text: Part of the gene associated with Huntington’s disease has a repeated DNA triplet nucleotide sequence of CAG. There are 35 or fewer CAG repeats in the normal allele. Alleles with 40 or more CAG repeats are expected to result in the development of Huntington’s disease.
The genetic screening test for Huntington’s disease includes a polymerase chain reaction (PCR). This results in amplification of the gene that is associated with Huntington’s disease.
The DNA fragments produced by PCR are then observed using agarose gel electrophoresis.

The genetic screening test results of four 18-year-old adults, A, B, C and D, who had no symptoms of Huntington’s disease are shown in Figure 3.1. Control DNA containing the fragments from amplification of alleles with 35 and 40 CAG repeats is also shown.

stem.caption: Figure 3.1
stem.alt: Gel with five lanes labelled adult A, adult B, adult C, adult D and control DNA, a well at the top of each lane, and an arrow labelled direction of DNA movement pointing down. Adult A: two bands close together near the bottom. Adult B: one band near the bottom and one band higher up. Adult C: one band near the bottom and one band about half way down. Adult D: one band near the bottom and one band close to the well. Control DNA: two bands in the lower half.

source.note: cropped from the PDF without the caption; caption kept as text

stem.text: The results of the tests were used to make predictions.

items: Adult B may or may not develop Huntington’s disease.
Adult C and adult D will develop Huntington’s disease.
Adult D will develop Huntington’s disease before adult C.

stem.text: Explain how the results of gel electrophoresis shown in Figure 3.1 support the predictions.

points.text: adult A has no alleles with more than 35 (CAG) repeats ; ora
adult B has one allele between 35 and 40 (CAG) repeats ;
adult C and adult D have one allele with more than 40 (CAG) repeats ;
adult D has more (CAG) repeats than adult C ;

guidance: A DNA fragments or bands for alleles throughout
markScheme.note: No “any X from” line: four points for four marks. In point 3 “and” is underlined in the MS (underline = the actual word must be used, MS p.7).

explanation.text: How to read the gel: DNA fragments move away from the wells in the direction of the arrow. Shorter fragments move further in the same time. More CAG repeats means a longer fragment, so the band is nearer the well.
Each adult has two alleles of the gene, and PCR copies both, so each lane can show up to two bands.

Use the control lane as a scale. The control band nearer the wells is the 40-repeat fragment; the one further away is the 35-repeat fragment. The figure does not label which band is which, so this follows from the rule above.

Compare each adult’s bands with the two control bands:
• A: both bands are further than the 35-repeat band, so neither allele has more than 35 repeats (MS point 1).
• B: one band lies between the two control bands, so one allele has between 35 and 40 repeats; this is why the prediction is “may or may not” (MS point 2).
• C and D: each has one band nearer the wells than the 40-repeat band, so each has one allele with more than 40 repeats. Because the allele is dominant, one such allele is enough (MS point 3).
• D’s upper band is nearer the wells than C’s, so D’s allele has more repeats (MS point 4).
The question does not say that more repeats leads to earlier onset. The prediction “D before C” together with MS point 4 shows that this is the link being tested.

reasoningChain: Shorter fragment → travels further; more CAG repeats → longer fragment → band nearer the well.
For each adult, compare the band nearer the well with the control bands.
A: no allele > 35 → will not develop. B: one allele 35–40 → may or may not.
C and D: one allele > 40 → will develop (one dominant allele is enough).
D’s band nearer the well than C’s → more repeats → earlier onset.

inferredMistakes.text: Reversing the rule and saying the band that travelled further has more repeats.
Writing about only C or only D for the third prediction. MS point 3 underlines “and”, so both adults are needed.

stem.text: Some genetic diseases, such as severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID), can be treated by gene therapy.
Explain why Huntington’s disease cannot be treated using the type of gene therapy used to treat SCID.

topics.note: Only relevant to the ER comment that some responses suggested gene editing; please confirm whether to keep.

points.text: addition of normal allele only corrects recessive disorders
alternatives: dominant allele cannot be, masked / switched off ;

points.text: gene therapy does not remove the, mutated / dominant, allele ;
not able to replace, nerve / brain cells ;
correct type of stem cells may not be available ; A correct ref. to viruses

explanation.text: What the SCID treatment does: it is gene addition. A normal allele is added to the patient’s cells; the faulty allele stays in the cells. This works for SCID because SCID is recessive: one working allele is enough to make the missing protein.

Why this fails for Huntington’s disease: the disease allele is dominant. Adding a normal allele does not remove the mutant allele (MS point 3), and the mutant allele still causes the disease even with a normal allele present. A dominant allele “cannot be masked” (MS point 2), which is the step the examiners say some responses did not fully explain.

The MS also credits ideas about the cells involved: the nerve or brain cells affected cannot simply be replaced, and a suitable type of stem cell may not be available (MS points 4 and 5). A correct reference to viruses (as vectors) is also accepted in point 5.

reasoningChain: SCID gene therapy adds a normal allele; it does not remove the faulty one.
SCID is recessive, so one added normal allele restores the function.
Huntington’s disease is dominant, so the mutant allele still has its effect and cannot be masked by an added normal allele.
Extra point: the affected cells are nerve / brain cells, which cannot be replaced, and the correct stem cells may not be available.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing gene therapy as “replacing” or “removing” the faulty allele. MS point 3 states that it does not remove it.
Stating that Huntington’s disease is recessive, which is the opposite of MS point 1.

shared.text: Two ideas run through parts (b) to (d): (1) Huntington’s disease is caused by a dominant allele of the HTT gene, so one mutant allele is enough to cause the disease; (2) the mutant allele has a larger number of CAG repeats (the question stem gives the thresholds: 35 or fewer is normal, 40 or more is expected to cause the disease).
